To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Tsr localizes to cell poles; (2) Tsr accumulation at the cell pole occurs linearly with time; (3) more Tsr is at the old pole than at the new pole; and (4) the level of Tsr at the old pole is roughly proportional to cell age.

the chemotaxis signal transduction protein Tsr accumulates linearly over time at the cell pole of Escherichia coli, and thus that the amount of Tsr at a cell pole can be reliably used as an indicator of cell age.

(1) Tsr–Gfp accumulates approximately linear with time at cell pole, and can be utilized to differentiate ‘old versus new’ cell pole; (2) the rate of Tsr–gfp accumulation is large enough for old and new pole to be distinguished even for cells whose pole has had only one generation for Tsr–Gpf accumulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of a chemotaxis receptor as a reporter of the age of Escherichia colipoles.
the use of Tsr–Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) as a marker of pole age and the use of T‐GFP‐labelled cells to investigate the relationship between cell age and chemotaxis behaviour.
the development of a tool to distinguish old and new poles of Escherichia coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Tsr is a ‘polarity factor’, in that it localizes to cell poles, but not a ‘polarity gene product’, in that its localization is not dependent on the cell's prior history.
the current study demonstrates that Tsr–Gfp can be used to reliably assign old and new poles to any E. coli cell, even when the prior history of the cell is not known.
Tsr–GPF accumulates linearly at cell poles with time, and can thus be used to differentiate old versus new poles, even in cells whose prior history has not been recorded.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, by virtue of the linear accumulation of Tsr– GFP at the cell poles, the pole‐localized Tser protein can be used to assign old and new poles to cells and to estimate cell age.
Tsr–Gfp accumulates linearly at poles, and can thus be used to distinguish old and new poles in E.coli, and thus can be used as a marker for pole age.
Tsr–Gfp accumulates linearly at the poles of cells with time, and thus can be reliably used as a pole‐age marker.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Tsr–Gfp can be used to reliably distinguish old and new poles, even for very young cells, in a manner that does not require knowledge of a cell’s prior history.
the pole localization of a protein, even one with a very low diffusion rate, can be used to distinguish between old and new poles.
the pole‐specific accumulation of Tsr– GFP is a robust, reproducible, and useful phenomenon, which should find application in studies of cell polarity and the regulation of protein localization.
